stories.headline: Njoku, Nwosu, Emmanwori, and more - 10 NFL players of Nigerian origin to watch this season
stories.summary: The NFL has long had a significant African presence, but no country is represented quite like Nigeria.
stories.body:
The 2026 NFL season is underway, and Nigerians will once again have plenty of reasons to pay attention, with players of Nigerian origin spread across the league, from defending Super Bowl champions to established starters, and former high draft picks looking for breakout seasons.

The NFL has long had a significant African presence, but no country is represented quite like Nigeria. There are 137 players of African origin across NFL rosters and practice squads at the start of the 2026 season, representing 24 African countries, with Nigeria accounting for 93 of them, more than two-thirds of the total.

Liberia is a distant second with nine players, followed by Côte d'Ivoire with seven, Cameroon with six and Ghana with five.

Every NFL team has at least one player of African origin, while Nigerian representation stretches across 29 of the league's 32 teams. Only the Minnesota Vikings, New Orleans Saints and Arizona Cardinals do not have a player of Nigerian origin on their roster or practice squad.

No team has more than the New York Jets. The Jets have eight players of Nigerian origin, including one on the practice squad, with Olu Fashanu, Joseph Ossai and Lagos-born veteran David Onyemata among the most recognizable.

Those numbers help illustrate how dramatically Nigeria's footprint in American football has grown. The country's NFL connection is no longer represented by a handful of isolated success stories.

Nigerian-born players and the children of Nigerian immigrants now occupy positions across the league, from quarterbacks and offensive linemen to linebackers, defensive backs and pass rushers.

Some are already champions. Uchenna Nwosu and Nick Emmanwori helped the Seattle Seahawks win Super Bowl LX last season, while Moro Ojomo and Osa Odighizuwa enter this year on NFC teams with legitimate championship ambitions.

Foye Oluokun remains one of the league's most productive linebackers, while former high draft picks Olu Fashanu and David Ojabo enter potentially important seasons in their development as potential breakout candidates.

Jalen Milroe, whose playing time may be considerably more limited but whose position, Nigerian heritage and presence on the defending champions make his development particularly intriguing.

Several others could have a significant say in who is still playing when Super Bowl LXI arrives in Los Angeles on Feb. 14.

From the contenders to the challengers and potential breakout players, here are 10 NFL players of Nigerian origin to watch in 2026.

SUPER BOWL CONTENDERS
Uchenna Nwosu, Edge, Seattle Seahawks
There is probably no better place to start than Nwosu. He is an established NFL veteran, a Super Bowl champion and a significant contributor on a Seattle team trying to win consecutive titles.

Nwosu played 16 games last season and recorded seven sacks, his best total since registering 9.5 in 2022.

He played 33 defensive snaps in Seattle's season-opening 13-10 victory over New England, finishing with five tackles and a pass defended as the Seahawks began their title defense by beating the team they defeated in Super Bowl LX.

At 29, Nwosu is entering a stage where another strong season and another championship run would add considerably to an already successful NFL career.

Why watch: An established Nigerian-American pass rusher playing significant snaps for the defending champions.

Super Bowl chances: Excellent.

Nick Emmanwori, Safety, Seattle Seahawks
Nwosu may be the established veteran, but Emmanwori could eventually become the bigger star. The young safety made an immediate impact as a rookie, finishing runner-up for AP Defensive Rookie of the Year and helping Seattle win the Super Bowl.

At 6-foot-3, Emmanwori possesses unusual size and athleticism for a safety, allowing Seattle to deploy him in multiple roles rather than simply leaving him deep in the secondary.

The challenge now is the second season. Opposing offenses have a full year of film on him, while expectations are considerably higher than when he arrived in the league. An offseason ankle problem also makes his health worth monitoring early in the season.

If healthy, Emmanwori has an opportunity to establish himself among the league's emerging defensive stars.

Why watch: He could make the jump from outstanding rookie to one of the NFL's better young defensive backs.

Super Bowl chances: Excellent.

Moro Ojomo, DT, Philadelphia Eagles
Ojomo has taken a very different route than usual to the NFL. Born in Lagos, he moved to California with his family when he was 8, eventually starred at Texas and was selected by the Philadelphia Eagles in the seventh round of the 2023 NFL draft.

For players selected that late, simply sticking around is an achievement. Ojomo has done considerably more. He has developed into an increasingly important part of an Eagles defensive front featuring Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, giving Philadelphia another source of interior pressure.

That development makes 2026 particularly interesting. Ojomo has already gone from seventh-round project to legitimate NFL contributor. Another step Up the ladder could make him a much more recognizable name beyond Philadelphia.

Why watch: One of the best development stories among Nigerian-born players in the NFL and now an important piece on a championship contender.

Super Bowl chances: Very good.

Osa Odighizuwa, DT, San Francisco 49ers
There are flashier names on this list, but few have been more dependable. Odighizuwa played all 17 games in each of his final four seasons with the Dallas Cowboys before moving to San Francisco, establishing himself as one of the league's more durable interior defensive linemen.

Odighizuwa also comes from a football family. His older brother Owamagbe played in the NFL and now Osa arrives in San Francisco with an obvious assignment.

The 49ers recorded an NFL-low 20 sacks last season and needed additional help for a defensive front that had lost some of its previous dominance. Odighizuwa provides an established interior presence alongside Nick Bosa.

His first game suggested that the opportunity will be substantial this season. He started at defensive tackle and recorded two tackles as San Francisco's defense overwhelmed the Rams in a 27-7 season-opening victory in Melbourne. They limited the Rams to just seven points and 290 total yards, forced two turnovers, and limited Matthew Stafford to 155 passing yards

With fellow starting tackle Alfred Collins lost for the season with a torn patellar tendon, Odighizuwa is now an even more important part of a 49ers defensive front attempting to return to its old standards.

Why watch: Proven durability, substantial playing time and a new role on a team expecting to contend.

Super Bowl chances: Very good.

CHALLENGERS
Michael Onwenu, OL, New England Patriots
Onwenu already knows how close the Patriots came. New England's 2025 season carried them all the way to Super Bowl LX before Seattle ended the run with a 29-13 victory.

Onwenu remains one of New England's most important offensive linemen and has provided valuable versatility throughout his career, playing both guard and tackle. His role becomes even more important with quarterback Drake Maye established as the centerpiece of the Patriots offense.

Onwenu began 2026 where he left off, starting at right guard as New England's rebuilt offensive line allowed just two sacks against Seattle in its 13-10 opening-night loss.

The Patriots still had problems dealing with Seattle's pressure, particularly late, but Onwenu remains the established presence on an offensive line charged with protecting Maye as New England attempts to return to the Super Bowl.

Why watch: An established Nigerian-American starter protecting one of the AFC's leading young quarterbacks.

Super Bowl chances: Very good.

David Njoku, TE, Los Angeles Chargers
Njoku provides something this Nigerian group otherwise lacks: an established offensive skill-position player, having built a substantial NFL career as an athletic receiving tight end and now begins a new chapter with the Los Angeles Chargers.

His production dipped last season, when he caught 33 passes for 293 yards and four touchdowns in 12 games, making his fresh start alongside Justin Herbert particularly interesting.

Why watch: A proven offensive player getting a fresh start with one of the NFL's established quarterbacks.

Super Bowl chances: Good.

Foye Oluokun, LB, Jacksonville Jaguars
If playing time and production were the only criteria, Oluokun would be much higher.

The linebacker has been one of the NFL's most prolific tacklers, including league-leading totals of 192 with Atlanta in 2021 and 184 in his first season with Jacksonville.

Oluokun is an established every-down linebacker and a central figure in Jacksonville's defense.

Why watch: Perhaps the safest bet among this entire group to accumulate substantial playing time and production.

Super Bowl chances: Outside chance.

POTENTIAL BREAKOUTS
Olu Fashanu, OT, New York Jets
The Jets selected Olumuyiwa Fashanu in the first round of the 2024 draft after an outstanding college career at Penn State, viewing the Nigerian-American tackle as a potential long-term cornerstone of their offensive line.

Eventually, draft position has to translate into production, and it is about time for that developmental period to give way to expectation.

Fashanu possesses the size, footwork and pedigree that made him one of the premier offensive-line prospects in his draft class. Now he needs to establish himself as a high-level NFL starter.

Why watch: Former first-round talent approaching a potentially defining stage of his development.

Super Bowl chances: It is the Jets...

David Ojabo, Edge, Miami Dolphins
Few players on this list have a wider range of possible outcomes than Ojabo. Born in Port Harcourt, Ojabo spent part of his childhood in Nigeria before moving to Scotland and eventually the United States.

He took up American football relatively late but developed so quickly at Michigan that he was projected as a potential first-round pick before tearing his Achilles at his pro day.

Injuries repeatedly interrupted his career in Baltimore, and Miami now provides another opportunity. At 26, there is still time to show that the physical talent which once made him one of college football's most intriguing edge defenders can translate consistently to the NFL.

Why watch: This could be a pivotal season for one of the most naturally talented Nigerian-born players in the league.

Super Bowl chances: Low.

Jalen Milroe, QB, Seattle Seahawks
Milroe is the wildcard of this selection. Incidentally, not many are even aware that he has Nigerian heritage, and only a deep dive into his full name, Jalen Oluwaseun Isaiah Milroe, would give it away.

His position, as one of only two quarterbacks of Nigerian origin in the league - the other being former Kansas City practice squad QB Chris Oladokun, who is now a free agent - makes his development worth following.

Milroe is not Seattle's starting quarterback, meaning he could play considerably fewer snaps than anybody else in this top 10. But he did get minutes last season, and quarterbacks operate under different rules.

Milroe's exceptional running ability gives Seattle the possibility of using him in specialized packages, while his longer-term development could eventually determine whether he gets an opportunity to become an NFL starter.

Why watch: A quarterback of Nigerian heritage with exceptional physical tools developing on the roster of the NFL champions.

Super Bowl chances: Excellent as a member of Seattle, although his individual role could be limited.

HONORABLE MENTIONS
Boye Mafe, Edge, Cincinnati Bengals: The Nigerian-American pass rusher leaves Seattle with a Super Bowl ring and joins a Cincinnati team capable of making noise in the AFC.

Odafe Oweh, Edge, Washington Commanders: Oweh is one of the more physically gifted pass rushers in the league. His cross-town move from Baltimore gives him another opportunity to translate those tools into consistent production.

Joseph Ossai, Edge, New York Jets: Lagos-born Ossai has shown disruptive ability without yet producing consistently enough to become a leading NFL edge defender.

David Onyemata, DT, New York Jets: Born in Lagos and introduced to organized American football after moving to Canada for university, Onyemata has fashioned a remarkable decade-long NFL career.

Olu Oluwatimi, C, Seattle Seahawks: Oluwatimi appeared in eight regular-season games with four starts before playing in all three games of Seattle's postseason championship run. He begins 2026 behind the starters, but could become important if injuries create an opportunity.

stories.headline: Aleksander Barkov appreciating Panthers return after lost season
stories.summary: In the mind of Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over.
stories.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- In the mind of Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over.

It happened in May, in a far-from-filled Swedish arena, when Barkov suited up for Finland in an exhibition against Switzerland for his first game since shredding his right knee in the Panthers' first training camp practice 7½ months earlier. On one of his first shifts, he tumbled to the ice.

Nothing bad happened.

"Very good news," Barkov said.

That was it. That was all it took for Barkov to realize his surgically repaired knee was good, that he could play without fear or concern. A few weeks later, he hoisted the trophy when Finland won the IIHF world championship.

Now he is home in Florida, set for the start of training camp and ready to lead a team that, even after missing the playoffs last season, has been set by most sportsbooks as the favorite to win what would be its third Stanley Cup in a four-year span.

"Don't take anything for granted," Barkov said, when asked what he learned from not being able to play for Florida last season. "You just have to enjoy every single chance you get to play hockey, to be with your teammates, to go to every single practice, every single game. You've got to be excited about that."

The Panthers, who were holding media day on Wednesday in advance of Thursday's first practice of camp, have plenty of reasons to be excited. Many core players from the runs to the Cup titles in 2024 and 2025 are back, names like Barkov, Matthew Tkachuk, Sam Reinhart, Sam Bennett, Aaron Ekblad, Carter Verhaeghe, Gustav Forsling, Brad Marchand, Anton Lundell, Dmitry Kulikov and Niko Mikkola.

Brady Tkachuk, Matthew's brother, has been added to the mix, and Florida even brought Radko Gudas -- a fan favorite from his first stint with the Panthers -- back to help shore up the defense. In net, with Sergei Bobrovsky gone to Toronto, Florida is turning the goaltender job over to Jacob Markstrom.

"Every single guy who has come in, they look so determined to be their best and to show their best," Barkov said. "But they also know that we're all in this together. Every single person is important, and every single has their own abilities to lead in their own way. We have many of those guys, so that's the best part of this. No one's here by themselves. Everyone can be just whatever they are."

That didn't happen last season. Injuries gutted the Panthers, starting with Barkov.

He got hurt about 20 minutes into the first practice of training camp, tearing the ACL and MCL in his right knee on Sept. 25, 2025. He had surgery a day later and was skating within a few months, but by the time he was ready to seriously consider returning to game action, Florida was out of playoff contention.

It wasn't entirely a lost season for Barkov. He missed the chance to serve as Finland's captain at the Milan Cortina Olympics but played for his country at the IIHF world championships in the spring and got to hoist the trophy when Finland beat host Switzerland 1-0 in the gold medal game.

Florida's career leader in goals and assists is raring to go with the Panthers once again.

"We all know camp is always going to be hard, no matter what. It's going to be hard physically and mentally," Barkov said. "We're all kind of ready for that test."

stories.headline: Barcelona, Real Madrid monitoring JJ Gabriel situation at Man United - sources
stories.summary: Barcelona and Real Madrid are among the clubs monitoring JJ Gabriel's stand-off with Manchester United, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
Barcelona and Real Madrid are among the clubs monitoring JJ Gabriel's stand-off with Manchester United, sources have told ESPN.

The 15-year-old and his representatives have stunned Old Trafford bosses by demanding to leave. United, according to sources, will not cancel his contract and he cannot be de-registered.

But Gabriel's stance has opened the door to a departure next summer. He's eligible to sign scholarship forms after his 16th birthday, which is on Oct. 6.

Spanish giants Barcelona and Real Madrid have both been alerted to the situation. Gabriel can move to a European side because he has an Irish passport.

Real Madrid's plan would be to play him in their B-team.

Sources have told ESPN that Premier League clubs including Manchester City and Chelsea are also closely watching developments.

However, one source close to a prominent English club said there's a feeling within the game that Gabriel will eventually agree a way back in at United.

United bosses are hopeful that the situation can still be rectified and insist they do not know the exact reasons behind his desire to leave.

- Michael Carrick faces rotation dilemma vs. Brighton amid Man United pressure

Gabriel was in line to be part of Michael Carrick's squad for the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton on Wednesday. Had he featured, he would have become United's youngest ever player.

However, the highly-rated teenager is now set to be left out after missing training this week.

stories.headline: Max vs 100: How Verstappen's karting years made an F1 champion - and prepared him for an all-new test
stories.summary: Max Verstappen tells ESPN's Laurence Edmondson how his karting roots shaped his F1 career and prepared him for the Max vs 100 challenge.
stories.body:
On Sept. 16, Max Verstappen will attempt to overtake 100 other drivers in a unique go-karting challenge at Silverstone, live on ESPN on Disney+. Ahead of the event, ESPN caught up with the four-time world champion to discuss his long history of go-karting and the years he spent honing his skills at tracks across Europe.

Between the ages of four and 15, Max Verstappen's life revolved around go-kart tracks.

Weekends would be spent racing all around Europe, initially close to home in Belgium and the Netherlands and then further afield in Italy, Spain and the U.K. in his early teens.

His father, Jos, a former Formula 1 driver, would load Max's kart into the back of their van ahead of every race weekend and drive his son across the length and breadth of Europe to the next event. During the height of Max's karting career, Jos calculated they were clocking up more than 60,000 motorway miles per year as the father-and-son team hoovered up trophies on a path destined for F1.

"It was a really nice period in my life," Max recalls. "All different kinds of conditions, tracks, travels.

- Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen

- Max vs 100: F1 drivers predict how Verstappen will fare racing 100 drivers

- What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records

"Sometimes it wasn't even the race weekend I loved the most, but just the travel experience together with my dad; in the van, talking a lot about life, talking a lot about the current, but also, of course, where we were trying to head to.

"For sure, go-karting has been a massive part of my life."

On weekdays, Jos would pick Max up after school and take him directly to his workshop to work on his kart engines. Max was encouraged to get his hands dirty from an early age, and the hours of tinkering after school would only come to an end when it was time to head home for dinner. Once they'd eaten, Max would go up to bed and Jos would return to the workshop, sometimes until midnight, until every last performance advantage had been found.

"My dad was my mechanic and my engine tuner as well," Max recalls. "We had our own dyno also in the workshop, so we did a lot in-house.

"I know a lot of dads are mechanics or they work with their son, but I don't know anyone that has done it so intensively.

"My dad really understood what was needed from the go-kart, but also from the engine."

The local kart circuit in Genk, Belgium became the Verstappens' second home. All through the year Max would take to the track multiple times a week to test new parts while learning to brake later, rotate the kart more precisely, and get on the throttle earlier.

Even in the wet winter months when other karters would pack up early and go home, the Verstappens would continue to clock up the mileage. Max would stay out on track until his hands felt frozen to the bone and he could barely feel his fingertips.

"I would warm my gloves on the exhaust because it's quite hot," he says with a smile. "You could put your gloves on it for a little bit and then take them off and they would be warm.

"It works really well, but the problem is when you're really cold and you heat them up your fingers swell up because of the increase of blood flow. Sometimes you were driving a bit with thick hands. But it all makes you tougher as a driver and as a kid at the time."

'You only get one shot at this'

The school Max was attending in Belgium didn't recognise go-karting as a sport, which made it difficult to get exemptions from class for races on the other side of Europe. When he did, the young Verstappen tried to focus on his homework during those 10- or 12-hour road trips in the van, but ultimately his schoolwork never came as easily as the karting trophies.

"It was tough. Sometimes I would come back home and you arrive on a Monday back, and you've kind of missed a week of lecturing and you try to catch up within two or three days of what was missed.

"With that already I didn't like school, so it was a bit tough.

"I always targeted to do something in life where school was not necessary. Plus, at the same time, I always said to myself, even if it doesn't work out in racing I can always go back to school.

"You only get one shot at this. If you fail because you try to catch up on school, I think I would always kick myself. School you can always catch up on."

It's hard to believe now, but early in Max's karting journey there was a moment when Jos wasn't sure if his son had the talent to make it all the way to F1. He had been karting for over a year and making steady progress, but then, ahead of his sixth birthday, the lap times stopped improving.

"I think there was a time when my dad was questioning it a little bit," Max says. "We always went to that same track in Genk, and at one point I stalled a little bit -- when you are four years old naturally there is a progression, but I think around five-and-a-half or six years old it was like I plateaued. We went again and again and again and I didn't really get faster.

"I just kept being a couple of tenths off what I needed to be, of the older guys because that is what you compare yourself to. Then my dad had a good idea. We went to a different track for the first time, so I drove somewhere new for the first time.

"It actually went really well on that particular track, so when I went back to Genk it also clicked and I suddenly just picked up pace.

"Maybe my mind needed a little reset of just seeing different corners and a different combination of corners.

"I spoke about it with my dad years later, but I remember the scene of going to Genk over and over again and going to that other track for the first time, I do remember that.

"At the time I didn't know that my dad was so worried about my pace, but I do remember the sequence because it went really well on that particular track. My dad was like, 'tomorrow we go again but to Genk.' I was like 'alright, sure. I drive wherever.'"

- Max vs 100 explained: Rules, drivers, shortcuts and how Verstappen can win

Was there ever a time when Max didn't enjoy the endless pursuit of lap time?

"I always loved it and I think you always want to go out and go fast," he says.

"But of course there are also moments where maybe it's not going so well. You don't love it to 100%. But at the end of the day I would always wake up the next day wanting to go.

"It's like in life. There are better days and there are worse days."

How Jos Verstappen prepared Max for F1

In Jos, Max had a mechanic, an engineer and a driver coach. Every time they arrived for a test session, there would be a plan to ensure every lap resulted in progress towards the end goal of winning the next race, fighting for the next championship, and inching closer to the dream of F1.

"When we went karting there was always a clear strategy behind it with my dad, in terms of what we were practicing," Max says.

"My dad never said to me 'just go out and have fun.' No, we go out because we're testing or preparing. There was always a very strict strategy behind it.

"Even when we would go on summer holidays, of course we would also spend time on the beach, but we had go-karting days where we would create mini races.

"So one time I would start first, then second, third, last. With however many people we were with, which was mainly 7-8 people maximum. So one time you start first, then last, or you're in the middle.

"We would create these little start scenarios and overtaking scenarios. It was really fun."

The nostalgia Max feels for those endless days of karting is almost tangible as he sits in Red Bull's F1 paddock hospitality. The dream he had as a kid was ultimately fulfilled in 2021 when he won his first Formula 1 title before going on to take three more over the following three years.

Now a father himself, it begs the question of whether he can see himself becoming a karting dad?

"You don't know," he says. "I think what is always very important as a parent is that you support them in whatever they want to do.

"It doesn't matter if you're a boy or a girl, but for me, I'm not going to be the parent that is going to push them into a racing scenario. If they want to do it, sure. I will make sure that she or he will have the best possibilities.

"But I'm not going to actively push it. They need to want it.

"I hope they do something else -- I hope they play tennis or play football!"

Max vs 100: Can Verstappen pass them all?

The freezing cold test days and overtaking drills during his summer holidays will likely come in useful next week as Max attempts to pass 100 karts on a specially designed kart track at Silverstone. The furthest back he can remember starting on a grid during his karting career was 10th or 11th and he hasn't driven a competitive go-kart since 2016 (his track days away from F1 are now firmly focused on GT racing).

"A hundred is a lot, you know, but I think how they've set up the track from what they've shown me, I think it will be good," Max says of the challenge. "But it's still going to be hectic, for sure."

And in terms of a strategy, will Max, to borrow one of his own phrases, go "full send"?

"I think I first need to understand and see the level between drivers.

"I also don't like to overthink the situation. I just need to go with the flow and try to make the best of it.

"I'm hoping that with my background, I should be faster than most. I hope! I mean, it would be quite embarrassing if they're faster than me!"

Max vs 100: When and how do I watch it?
Max vs 100 is taking place on Sept. 16, and will be shown live in the UK on Disney+.

In the U.S., Max vs 100 will also air on the ESPN App for Unlimited subscribers before a delayed ESPN2 broadcast later that day.

The race itself will start at 6 p.m., with the live stream beginning one hour before.

Comedian Mo Gilligan will front the coverage, which is set to include drone footage and live race data.

Stream Max vs 100 globally on ESPN on Disney+ on Wednesday, Sept. 16. Coverage starts at 5 p.m. BST, before the race begins at 6 p.m.

stories.body:
Preliminary final weekend begins with a huge clash between Sydney and Fremantle at the SCG, before Brisbane travel to face Hawthorn in a twilight clash at the MCG.

Keep up to date with all of the fixtures, games, ins and outs, team news, tips, odds, results, reaction, and video as they come to hand.

FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 18

Sydney vs. Fremantle
SCG, 7:40pm [AEST]

Team news: Sydney coach Dean Cox has plenty to think about this week when it comes to selection. Key forward Joel Amartey is fit and available after suffering an Achilles injury in the middle of the season, while important wingman Justin McInerney (hamstring) is also expected to be considered if he gets through training unscathed. The forced inclusion does come at the expense of Callum Mills, who unfortunately ruptured his ACL during the qualifying final win over Brisbane. For the Dockers, Brennan Cox could be the heartbreak story of preliminary final week, with the defender not travelling to Sydney for Friday night's clash at the SCG. Cox will instead line up for Peel Thunder in Sunday's WAFL grand final against Claremont.

ESPN tip: Dockers by 14 points

Pointsbet odds: Swans $2.45, Dockers $1.55

Get your tips in now on the ESPNfootytips app!

SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 12

Hawthorn vs. Brisbane
MCG, 5:15pm [AEST]

Team news: Brisbane spearhead Logan Morris finished the semifinal win over Adelaide on the bench with ice on his calf, though it's believed that was a precautionary measure given the win was all but assured. Still, there'll be a watch on how he trains this week. Defender Noah Answerth will be doing all he can to return from an ankle injury after he missed the Crows game, but he'll need to prove his fitness and it's hard to find a likely omission. "I'm not sure that Noah's fit," coach Chris Fagan said. "He wasn't able to run last week, so we'll see how he goes this week. "That's one that we'll know more about as the week goes on."

ESPN tip: Hawks by 7 points

stories.headline: Knicks agree to deal with veteran free agent John Konchar
stories.summary: John Konchar agreed to a one-year deal with the New York Knicks, agent George S. Langberg of GSL Sports Group told ESPN on Tuesday night.
stories.body:
Free agent forward John Konchar agreed to a deal with the New York Knicks, agent George S. Langberg of GSL Sports Group told ESPN on Tuesday night.

Konchar, 30, is entering his eighth NBA season after spending 2025-26 with the Utah Jazz and Memphis Grizzlies.

The Knicks have two open roster spots and Konchar has a strong opportunity to make New York's final roster, sources said. The Knicks also plan to sign center Drew Eubanks to a deal to compete for a roster spot, sources said.

Konchar was one of the most experienced free agents remaining on the market, with over 360 games in the NBA under his belt. He spent the first six seasons of his career with Memphis before he was traded midseason to the Jazz.

He averaged 5.9 points, 3.0 assists and 5.7 rebounds in 26 games for Utah last season.

stories.headline: Cristian 'Kily' González arrives to take charge of Messi, Miami
stories.summary: New Inter Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" González said he feels blessed at being given the opportunity to lead the club and coach Lionel Messi, after formerly taking up the role on Tuesday.
stories.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- New Inter Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" González said he feels blessed at being given the opportunity to lead the club and coach Lionel Messi, after formerly taking up the role on Tuesday.

González has now received the authorization to begin the job after being announced last month as the permanent replacement for interim coach Guillermo Hoyos on a contract through June 2028.

- Source: Colombia targeting U.S. U20 dual national Shaw

- Messi tracker: All goals, assists, key moments for Miami, Argentina in 2026

- Messi scores, but Nashville strikes late to deny Miami win

The job sees him reunite with Messi after the two shared the field for Argentina in two World Cup qualifiers in 2005.

"There are things in football that simply cannot be described in words; they are unique feelings. I feel privileged and blessed to have this opportunity and to share the fantastic relationship I have with Leo," González said in a news conference.

"I adore him, he knows it, and that makes this moment even more special. Being with him and sharing experiences with the incredible players on this squad. Honestly, as a coach, I feel completely fulfilled.

"Of course, this is all wonderful, but now we have to get to work. God willing, we'll start off strong tomorrow and win the championship."

González led his first training session with Inter Miami on Tuesday after landing in Miami from Argentina earlier in the morning. He will be on the sidelines for the team's Campeones Cup match against Liga MX champions Cruz Azul on Wednesday night at Nu Stadium.

Inter Miami reached an agreement with González on Aug. 27, but the coach could not take over for Hoyos until receiving his work permit.

"What were these past few days like? To be honest, they were filled with a lot of anticipation. It had been nearly two and a half weeks and I couldn't be here, but this unique opportunity, something I hadn't even dared to dream of, became a reality," González said.

"We spoke with the club, and they offered me the chance to join the team; I said yes immediately. Being with the players, seeing their willingness to welcome my coaching staff, and watching them train the way they did today honestly, it made me very happy and gave me a huge boost of energy for tomorrow's match."

Miami's opponent in the Campeones Cup was delayed in arriving in Miami for the game and instead of landing in the U.S. on Monday, were unable to fly in until Tuesday.

"Well, more than an odyssey, sometimes accidents like this happen, and you just have to turn the page," said Cruz Azul manager Joel Huiqui. "The team is doing well. We rested very well yesterday, we stayed at a hotel in Mexico, and we're just arriving now. We're calm, obviously aware that tomorrow will be a huge match for us, and we're all focused.

"It goes without saying that [Messis] is a great player, but what matters most to me is that the team realizes what is at stake: not just another trophy, but our consolidation as an institution. Beyond the chance to face a great player, the opportunity to win the title against a team like Inter Miami is about solidifying the work we've been doing and, above all, bringing joy to the fans."

Inter Miami currently sits in second place on the Eastern Conference table with 45 points in 25 games. The team has recorded just one victory in its last nine games.

Inter Miami forward Luis Suárez said he wants to use the game against Cruz Azul to start strong under new leadership.

"When it comes to playing a match like this, it's a final. There is no time to dwell on the past, the only thing that matters is looking ahead to tomorrow," Suárez said. "We've come through a challenging run of games, but now we face the best possible scenario: playing a final and moving forward with a new coach who brings great positive energy, a strong desire to grow and plenty of enthusiasm.

"That attitude is contagious, and we are ready to support him and his coaching staff."

Inter Miami hosts Cruz Azul before returning to Major League Soccer regular season action on Sunday against San Diego.

stories.headline: UFC's Islam Makhachev questions validity of Jon Jones' wins streak
stories.summary: UFC champ Islam Makhachev believes Jon Jones' failed drug tests and issues outside the Octagon invalidate Jones' place among the UFC's all-time streaks for consecutive wins.
stories.body:
Jon Jones and Islam Makhachev, two of the greatest fighters in UFC history, are taking shots at each other this week.

Makhachev (29-1) broke the UFC's official win streak record in August, when he defended his welterweight championship against Ian Machado Garry for his 17th consecutive win. Former middleweight champion Anderson Silva held the previous record of 16. Jones, a former light heavyweight and heavyweight champion, would argue he won 20 bouts in a row from 2010 to 2024, but his streak was interrupted by a no-contest against Daniel Cormier in 2017.

In a recent interview with a Russian news outlet, Makhachev said Jones' no-contest, which was the result of a failed drug test by the United States Anti-Doping Agency, invalidates his win streak.

"I'm not denying that Jon Jones is one of the greatest athletes in history, but he was caught doping twice," Makhachev told Ushatayka. "I think that's why his streak isn't considered valid. Because he went into a fight while on PEDs and won, that's where a new count should have started."

Jonse (28-1) was fined and suspended 15 months for testing positive for extremely trace amounts of steroid metabolites. He initially defeated Cormier in their fight in 2017, before it was later changed to a no-contest.

An independent arbitrator later stated he believed Jones unknowingly ingested the substance and that it was not performance enhancing. Jones has long pointed to that independent finding as validation of his innocence, and did so again Monday in a post directed at Makhachev.

"If you believe USADA for finding a picogram in my system, then you must believe USADA when they say it 'It was not found to be PERFORMANCE ENHANCING or INTENTIONAL,'" Jones wrote on X. "You can't have it both ways. Last I checked, my hand got raised every time I was in the Octagon since any of you can remember. Your own coach said I was 'a gift from God.' Let's not forget you've been KO'd, flatlined, went night night."

Makhachev, whose only loss came by knockout to Adriano Martins in his second UFC fight in 2015, responded to Jones the following day, and hinted at Jones's troubled legal history, both in and out of competition.

"Jon, I'm not trying to diminish your achievements in any way," Makhachev wrote on X. "But your whole life seems to be tied to breaking the rules one way or another, and somehow, you're never the one to be blamed."

stories.headline: Warriors sell out Eden Park in 48 hours amid NRL's crowd woes
stories.summary: Hooker Sam Healey plans to draw inspiration from his rugby league idol to help him handle the pulsating atmosphere of a sold-out Eden Park.
stories.body:
Hooker Sam Healey plans to draw inspiration from his NRL idol to help him handle the pulsating atmosphere of a sold-out Eden Park.

The NRL announced that general-public tickets for Sunday's do-or-die semi-final between the Warriors and Newcastle in Auckland had sold out in less than 48 hours.

It comes after New Zealand were forced to relocate from their traditional home ground for the clash because Eden Park hosts about 25,000 more spectators than Go Media Stadium.

The 50,000-seat venue being full comes after the league was criticised over poor crowd numbers in the first week of finals, although the Warriors had a mostly sold-out attendance for their 26-16 loss to the Dolphins.

Regardless, it's the club's first clash at Eden Park since 2014, and will be a mammoth moment for New Zealand rugby league as the Warriors look to keep alive their hopes of a first premiership.

Healey is yet to play at the venue, but will be wanting to produce similar heroics to his idol Kevin Locke, who made a courageous try-saving tackle on Sydney Roosters centre Michael Jennings at the Fortress in 2013.

"I have played league since I was five or six or something like that, so I always loved the game," Healey said.

"I actually saw him (Locke) in the sheds the other day, and I said to my mum, 'Do you remember when he was my favourite player'. She just started laughing.

"He used to be my lock-screen on my phone ... I just said g'day."

Warriors back-rower Jacob Laban has only played once at the country's biggest sporting stadium.

"It was Kiwi A's versus Tonga A's, I think it was two, three years ago," he said.

"(After) New Zealand played Samoa (in the Pacific Championships) ... it was a pretty cool, good atmosphere.

"Obviously it (the crowd) is a little bit further (away) than Mt Smart, but it's not too bad. When you score a try, you can walk up to the fans over there, so it's still pretty close."

Laban won't be intimidated by the history of Eden Park, although the club has won only one of its six games at the venue.

The blond second-rower is intent on not just helping the Warriors set up a preliminary final against Penrith, but also on making his childhood self proud.

"I knew I wanted to play for the Warriors when I first heard about rugby league," Laban said.

"They came to Wellington. I don't know what year it was, but I still have this photo of me where I had half a Warriors face painted on and a Warriors T-shirt.

"I knew I wanted to play for the Warriors since I was young."

stories.headline: NFL Week 2 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips
stories.summary: What's the latest for three teams dealing with QB injuries? What are we hearing on the Rams and Chargers after bad losses? And which Week 1 debuts stood out?
stories.body:
The 2026 NFL season is officially rolling. As we head into Week 2, insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

Week 1 saw the Seahawks, Vikings and Falcons all forced to turn to backup quarterbacks -- and in Atlanta's case, it was a third-stringer. Where do those franchises sit at QB entering Week 2? Jeremy and Dan also asked around about a tough opening week for the two Los Angeles teams. Is there concern yet for the Rams and Chargers? Plus, they debated debuts for coaches and rookies then offered up their best fantasy tips based on what they're hearing.

It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions heading into Week 2.

Jump to:

QB situations | Rams, Chargers concerns

Coaching debuts | Rookie debuts

Fantasy football takes

What's the latest on the quarterback situation for the Vikings, Seahawks and Falcons?
Graziano: Things seem straightforward for Minnesota. Based on what I've been able to gather, my sense is that Kyler Murray will start if he clears concussion protocol in time, and Carson Wentz is likely to start if Murray isn't clear in time. That sounds like a negative toward J.J. McCarthy, since it was him and not Wentz who competed with Murray for the starting job in camp. But this is more about the Vikings believing Wentz's veteran experience puts them in better position with limited preparation time when a QB gets hurt in-game (as happened Sunday) and/or there's uncertainty about who's going to start throughout the week.

McCarthy was the emergency third QB on Sunday, so the team knew there was a chance they might have to play him. I could see a scenario in which Wentz starts this week with McCarthy as the backup, assuming Murray can't go.

Fowler: That's certainly plausible. Murray took a nasty hit, and teams tend to be overly cautious when a player has assumed the fencing position, for good reason. But how players work through the five stages of the protocol often varies, so it's tough to know Murray's timeline at this point. Wentz is set up for success in Week 2. He got hot last week versus Green Bay, and Chicago just allowed 361 passing yards to Bryce Young.

In Seattle, it's clear Sam Darnold will miss this week and possibly Week 3. But the Seahawks have refrained from putting him on short-term injured reserve, which is a good sign. The team seems confident that Drew Lock is plug and play until Darnold returns.

Graziano: Yeah, Seattle believes Lock can handle it, so he's the guy there for the foreseeable future. I'm personally interested to see whether they put in anything specific for Jalen Milroe in terms of plays or packages that take advantage of his running ability and maybe give their offense a little bit extra juice. Why not, if Milroe is going to be active anyway as the second quarterback?

What about Atlanta? Kevin Stefanski probably thought he left the QB mess behind in Cleveland, but he has a situation on his hands, no?

Fowler: Stefanski has seen it all at quarterback, but at least his signal-callers in Cleveland mostly stayed out of the training room. Tua Tagovailoa's body seems to be betraying him at an inopportune time. The Falcons' best option remains third-year man Michael Penix Jr., but he's not yet ready for live game action. Penix wants to be fully confident before stepping onto the field following left ACL surgery in November. And my understanding is the Falcons are leaving the comfort level part of his recovery up to him.

Tagovailoa's injury, an oblique strain, can linger, which puts his Week 2 status up in the air. So, Cooper Rush starting another week wouldn't be shocking. What helps Tagovailoa's case is his accuracy, which Stefanski highly values. If Tagovailoa's body doesn't totally break down in the short term and he can return before Penix is ready, perhaps Tagovailoa can provide a spark.

Graziano: Penix is coming off his third ACL reconstruction, which is a lot of ACL reconstructions. I believe it takes a lot of mental work to convince yourself it's OK to go back out there and play. If Penix needs more time, I'm sure the Falcons will give it to him, though I believe we will see him on the field at some point this season. The Falcons are going to want to know whether he is a real long-term option moving forward.

My sense is Tagovailoa was the favorite to start at the beginning of camp even when Penix was healthy but that Tagovailoa didn't perform the way the team had hoped he would. That has turned things into a confusing mess.

Fowler: That two-week stretch, from the second preseason game rolling into the joint practice with the Colts, was rough for Tagovailoa. The schedule provides another wrinkle. Atlanta will play on Thursday night in Week 3, so even if Penix is close, that might not be the best week to reacclimate him.

How high is the panic level in the Rams' building? What about for the Chargers?
Fowler: Well, the Rams' top-ranked offense scored seven points, and the league's best pass rusher is out at least a month. But other than that, everything's fine! I don't, however, sense heavy panic from the Rams, who seemed to approach the Australia trip with the excitement of a teenager asked to take out the trash. 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris knows the Rams' offense well, so San Francisco's ability to stymie Matthew Stafford shouldn't be a total shock.

The Myles Garrett situation is more alarming. The Rams thought they could manage his knee injury with rest all camp and preseason, and it got exposed in Week 1. It leaves some uneasiness that they perhaps should have had this injury surgically repaired a tad sooner. But the Rams have plenty of defensive talent to offset the Garrett loss.

Graziano: Garrett missed basically an entire month's worth of training camp with the knee problem, so those of us on the outside should have considered that a possible warning sign, at the very least. Aaron Donald being able to play Monday night would help, but the issues that came up in Australia went beyond Garrett's health. The Rams' expensive new cornerback tandem looked miscast in the defensive game plan, and they couldn't get the passing game clicking.

The Rams are certainly not going to panic because of one game, even if it was an embarrassing loss to a division rival. But they are (and should be) taking the problems that were on display against the 49ers seriously. The operation needs to be sharper on both sides of the ball. One possible benefit of the Rams' controversial Australian travel plan is that they likely didn't need to get reacclimated upon their return home, since their body clocks theoretically never reset in the first place. We'll see if they come out looking sharper in Week 2 against the Giants.

Fowler: The Chargers' panic meter will rise if they lose to the Raiders this week. Arizona was deemed terrible in the preseason, but the Cardinals are more respectable than that, particularly on offense. So, the Chargers' defense gets a mulligan after seeing the Cards in the opener. It's a veteran group that should improve.

The bigger concern is how the Bolts' offense looked after wide receiver Ladd McConkey left the game with a rib injury. McConkey and Justin Herbert showed easy chemistry in that first half. They need McConkey, who is listed as day-to-day, to work his way back or concerns about the offensive attack will mushroom. I'm expecting a better running game from Los Angeles in Week 2 as it tries to find some continuity with the offensive line.

Graziano: McConkey is a great player, but the game plan falling apart completely once he exited makes it seem as if it was flimsy to begin with. Where are the smart, creative run plays Mike McDaniel was calling last season in Miami? Wasn't running back Omarion Hampton supposed to explode in this scheme? Wasn't the wide receiver group supposed to be deep with talent? Were the Chargers gaslighting us all summer? This was so far off our expectations for the Herbert-McDaniel pairing that you have to wonder whether L.A. took the Cardinals seriously enough.

But you're absolutely right, Jeremy. The Chargers need to beat the Raiders this week and look good doing it or we're going to wonder if it was all hype. Being 0-2 and looking up at the 2-0 Raiders in the AFC West standings would not feel good for a team that had the preseason hopes the Chargers held. But Raiders edge rusher Maxx Crosby isn't going to make life any easier on that offensive line, which struggled with protection in the first game.

Which new coach's debut surprised you the most in Week 1?
Graziano: The Cardinals' Mike LaFleur. I figured they'd have a representative offense, because I believe LaFleur is a talented offensive mind who knows how to call a game and put his players in the best position to take advantage of their strengths. But Arizona was good all over the field and dictated the action for much of Sunday's game. That says a lot about what LaFleur has been able to establish in terms of confidence and buy-in in a short period of time. Very impressive.

Fowler: It's early, but LaFleur seems to have a good sense of what it takes to be successful, with a blend of hard-nosed coaching and relatability that comes out in his news conferences and on the sidelines. I'd caution that Arizona started 2-0 last season before cratering, but its operation looks improved overall.

I was surprised Cleveland didn't play better under Todd Monken. Maybe I shouldn't have been since the offense is so young (six first- or second-year starters). But the 60-year-old Monken has waited decades for this opportunity, and his entire team was flat in Jacksonville. The outcry from fans will only intensify if quarterback Deshaun Watson plays poorly again.

Graziano: It's hard for me to be surprised when someone who insists on starting Watson at quarterback in 2026 doesn't have success. There are some things to like about Cleveland's roster, and I believe Monken knows how to coach, but the Browns aren't going anywhere with Watson. Until they admit that and make a change, I don't see how things can improve. Just horrendous vibes all the way around.

I have to say that Buffalo's Joe Brady probably had the best Week 1 win of the new coaches, prevailing on the road against Houston. Having spent a little time around the Bills before and after Sunday's game, it feels as if Brady is connecting with that group on a level that goes beyond his abilities as an offensive playcaller.

Fowler: Also, Jesse Minter winning his first game as the Ravens' coach wasn't a surprise, but the fashion in which his squad bounced Indianapolis was. Baltimore's offense was in complete control, and the defense forced two turnovers. Minter is known as a teacher/tactician, and the Ravens embodied that approach with minimal mistakes in Week 1.

Which rookie debut is drawing the most hype around the league?
Fowler: The first-year edge rushers flashed. David Bailey came out hot for the Jets, which was no surprise in league circles. "He was the most polished pass rusher [in the draft], so he had the best chances to contribute early among the top rushers," an NFL personnel director said. And it was quite the contribution, as Bailey registered four tackles, six quarterback pressures and one sack in 34 defensive snaps against Tennessee. Speaking of rookie rushers, the Chiefs' R Mason Thomas recorded his first sack on a spin move Monday night versus Denver. Thomas' buzz in Kansas City is growing due to his high motor and pass-rush arsenal.

Graziano: Buccaneers linebacker Josiah Trotter was tough to miss in his debut, with a sack and an interception return for a touchdown. Tampa Bay's second-round pick outshined Bucs first-rounder Rueben Bain Jr., who had a tough time against massive Bengals right tackle Amarius Mims. I've also heard positive reviews on the debut of Giants guard Francis Mauigoa, who was part of a bruising rushing attack against the Cowboys on Sunday night.

Fowler: Good call on Trotter. On the offensive side of the ball, Seahawks first-round running back Jadarian Price drew attention by the way he runs, not necessarily his modest Week 1 output (10 rushes, 52 yards). "He's a load," an AFC scout said. "I expect his profile to grow." Seattle has been very pleased with Price's acumen and has no problem getting him involved, though it is dedicated to a multiple-back approach. Ravens first-round guard Olaivavega Ioane looked imposing in Indianapolis. And third-round Dolphins wide receiver Caleb Douglas' five-catch, 94-yard debut confirmed what I was hearing: that Douglas had impressed everyone in Miami's building.

Graziano: For sure on Douglas! Love it when camp buzz comes to life in Week 1. Commanders' third-round wideout Antonio Williams was less buzzy, but it seems as if he has a real role as a slot receiver, and he caught a touchdown pass in his debut. I foresee Williams' role growing in that offense as the season goes along.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?
Graziano: I'd be trying to trade Houston running back David Montgomery. Yes, he had three touchdowns in his Texans debut. If you really believe he will score three touchdowns every week, you should not trade him for anything. I personally do not think he's going to do that.

I'm looking at Montgomery's 3.0 yards per carry against a Bills defense that was miserable against the run last season and the fact that Woody Marks was on the field for 40 snaps as compared with Montgomery's 39. The Texans were very impressed with the way Marks performed during the offseason, and they plan a significant role for the ball carrier in the offense. Montgomery got the Week 1 glory, but this might be a chance to sell high and claim a Week 1 underperformer who has a chance to pop in the coming weeks.

Fowler: Stick with Carolina wide receiver Jalen Coker (though maybe not this week). It would be silly to expect Coker to regularly break off 33-plus points like he did in Week 1, but he's clearly part of the Panthers' offensive fabric alongside wideout Tetairoa McMillan. Coker is a primary deep threat, and quarterback Bryce Young trusts him. Coker was a good value play before the Week 1 breakout. He is nursing an ankle sprain, which is something to consider for Week 2, but the Panthers' offense appears set for a jump, and Coker will be part of that. Carolina's coaches are very high on him.

stories.headline: Champion Hurricanes give captain Jordan Staal, 38, new deal
stories.summary: Veteran forward Jordan Staal, 38, who captained the Carolina Hurricanes to a Stanley Cup title in June, winning the Conn Smythe Trophy for postseason MVP along the way, signed a one-year contract extension with the club late Tuesday night.
stories.body:
Veteran forward Jordan Staal, who captained the Carolina Hurricanes to a Stanley Cup title in June, signed a one-year contract extension with the club Tuesday night.

Staal's deal now runs through the 2027-28 season, and it will pay a base salary of $900,000, with a $4 million signing bonus and up to $5.1 million in additional performance bonuses, the team announced in a statement.

"Jordan is not only our captain, he's the bedrock of the culture we've established in this organization," Hurricanes general manager Eric Tulsky said in the release. "His leadership, and on-ice performance throughout last season, and especially in the playoffs, was a primary factor in bringing the Stanley Cup back to Raleigh."

Staal, 38, finished the regular season with 20 goals and 36 points in 75 games, as the Hurricanes won the Metropolitan Division. He added eight goals and 12 points in 19 playoff games en route to securing the Conn Smythe Trophy as the most valuable player in the postseason.

A native of Thunder Bay, Ontario, Staal enters this season with 747 career points. He was the NHL's No. 2 pick by the Pittsburgh Penguins in 2006.

stories.headline: Roberto De Zerbi on misfiring Tottenham: 'We are going to win many games and score many goals'
stories.summary: Roberto De Zerbi has said that when his Tottenham Hotspur team clicks, they "are going to win many games and score many goals."
stories.body:
Roberto De Zerbi has said that when his Tottenham Hotspur team clicks, he believes they "are going to win many games and score many goals."

The Spurs head coach was speaking after Spurs were knocked out of the Carabao Cup with a 3-1 loss to Liverpool on Tuesday. Four games into the new Premier League season, Tottenham are still searching for their first goal of the campaign.

Conor Gallagher's second-half header at Anfield was the first goal Spurs have scored against top-flight opposition this season.

Despite the scoreline, Tottenham did edge Liverpool on xG (2.34 vs. 1.53), possession (56% vs. 44%), shots (17 vs. 12) and shots on target (6 vs. 5) and De Zerbi said that he sees signs that things are coming together for his new-look team.

"We have to be stronger," De Zerbi said. "I think last season was a school. I think it has to be a school for everyone. Now we are unlucky, because it's clear we have to improve many, many things, but also this night we played well, we created more chances, we shot more times, we got more corners than Liverpool. We could score more goals.

"I remember six, seven clear chances to score. Lucas Bergvall, Kudus and Udogie. In the second half, a couple with Marmoush, one Sávio, one Bergvall, another corner. I can't say nothing today.

"Now, my focus is on Villa and we have to prepare our best in the next game with this mentality to find this click.

"We are suffering because the results are our life, no? If we lose, we are sorry, we are sad, we are disappointed, we are frustrated. It's tough, no? But it's the first moment, the first part of this new project. I think when we make the click... but the click is not mentality, because today we showed the right mentality, the right behaviour and we played until the end of the game. I think we are going to win many games and score many goals."

- Liverpool's Iraola lauds Szoboszlai for 'worldie' in win over Spurs

- All 20 Premier League teams ranked: Which managers will be fired first?

Tottenham host also-winless Aston Villa in north London on Saturday in their next fixture and the Spurs boss has called on his team to sharpen up in the final third.

"We have to shoot more times and we have to shoot better and we have to finish better the clear situations but we are sorry for the result, disappointed, frustrated," he said.

"We have to be stronger in these unlucky moments because I am honest with myself and with you. I think this five or six games we have been for sure not lucky.

"I believe in my players, I have a big opinion of them and when we arrive to finally click to win a game we will enjoy it with these players because the look of the players is incredible.

"It is a tough moment but we have to be stronger."

stories.headline: Max vs 100 explained: Rules, drivers, shortcuts and how Verstappen can win
stories.summary: Everything you need to know ahead of Max v 100 at Silverstone, as Max Verstappen takes on a unique new challenge.
stories.body:
In one of the most unique challenges ever faced by a Formula 1 driver, Max Verstappen is taking to Silverstone on Wednesday, where he will try to overtake 100 drivers in just 30 laps.

Verstappen first sat in a kart at the age of four and was taking part in competition by the age of seven -- but has been in Formula 1 for the past 11 years.

He's set to roll back the years and test his go-karting pedigree once more against drivers from the world of social media, TV and sport.

Here's everything you need to know about Max vs 100.

- Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen

- Max vs 100: F1 drivers predict how Verstappen will fare racing 100 drivers

- How Verstappen's karting years prepared him for an all-new test

What is Max vs 100?
Max vs 100 is a one-off go-kart race organised by Red Bull, which sees four-time Formula 1 world champion Max Verstappen attempt to beat 100 amateur drivers from around the world at Silverstone.

What does Verstappen have to do to win?
Verstappen will start from the back of the grid, with all 100 competitors ahead of him. He will have 30 laps to overtake all of them in order to win.

When a kart is overtaken by Verstappen, they are out, meaning Verstappen could win before the 30 laps are complete.

What is the 'fast lap' and how do the shortcuts work?
Anyone attempting to hold off one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers of all time will need a little bit of help, and Max vs 100 competitors will have access to a 'fast lap' once during the race.

Drivers will be able to use their 'fast lap' at any time in the first 15 laps of the race, which will enable to them to take a shortcut on the track and gain some ground back on Verstappen when he begins to close in.

However, Verstappen has one available of his own to gain time -- but he cannot use it until the last 15 laps.

How does qualifying work?
The grid order will be determined by one flying lap around the specially-designed course at Silverstone -- with just a single attempt available. Much like in Formula 1, the grid order will be determined by lap times.

Are all the karts the same?
Every kart is identical. The complete weight, including driver and kit, must reach 85kg, meaning ballast will be added to karts which do not reach the total, levelling out the field.

Who are the 100 drivers facing Verstappen?
Among the drivers taking on Verstappen are personalities from TV, social media, and sport, though no professional racing drivers are included.

The list includes streamers Pieface, Caedrel and TheDonato, ultrarunner Arda Saatçi, basketball shooting phenomenon Chris "Lethal Shooter" Matthews, and 2019 Love Island winner Amber Gill.

Verstappen will be able to communicate with the field directly during the race, offering an insight into his racing brain.

How difficult will Max vs 100 be?
Verstappen's challenge in this race will not be in terms of raw pace or lap times, where he is certain to be a cut above the rest.

The issues will come in the form of traffic -- with so many karts ahead of him and some very likely to be lapped -- and time management, as Verstappen will need to calculate where and when he is to attempt passes.

A few of the field, while not professional, are karting influencers who know how to get round a track, and will want to make the most of their opportunity to defend against a Formula 1 icon.

When and how do I watch it?
Max vs 100 is taking place on Sept. 16, and will be shown live globally on ESPN on Disney+.

In the U.S., Max v 100 will also air on the ESPN App for Unlimited subscribers before a delayed ESPN2 broadcast later that day.

The race itself will start at 6 p.m., with the live stream beginning one hour before.

Comedian Mo Gilligan will front the coverage, which is set to include drone footage and live race data.

Stream Max vs 100 globally on ESPN on Disney+ on Wednesday, Sept. 16. Coverage starts at 5 p.m. BST, before the race begins at 6 p.m.
